findings: critical

Reviewer error or invalid verdict now returns 0 (pass) instead of 2 (block), so the gate fails open. (1) Attacker needs only to cause a reviewer outage, timeout, schema drift, or malformed output; no special access is required, and ordinary network flakiness triggers it. (2) Unreviewed or blocking-flagged code passes the review gate as "clean", which breaks the fail-closed invariant for every plugin user. (3) Cheapest fix: revert line 11 to `return 2`. Full fix: also add a regression test asserting that `error=True` and `valid=False` each return 2, and audit-log the failure reason. (gate.py:11)
medium

No test covers the error/invalid branch, so this fail-open inversion could land without anything turning red. (1) Nothing; this is a process gap. (2) Future silent regressions of the same fail-closed path. (3) Cheapest fix: a parametrized test on `check_review` for error, invalid, blocking and clean inputs. Full fix: a mutation test that asserts the gate goes red when this branch returns 0. (gate.py:10)
low

The error/invalid path returns without writing an audit record, so a reviewer outage leaves no trace of why the gate decided as it did. (1) The same reviewer failure as above. (2) Silent bypass that is not visible in the audit log. (3) Cheapest fix: log `result.error` and the validity state before returning. Full fix: route every non-clean outcome through the common audit writer. (gate.py:10)
high

Config `exclude` is checked before `HARD_PATHS`, so `.codex-gate.yaml` can declassify hard code paths. (1) The attacker must already be able to write `.codex-gate.yaml`, whether committed, unstaged, or in the worktree, which any repo contributor or an agent session can do. (2) They gain fail-open: a gate or deploy file in HARD_PATHS gets `is_code_path=False`, so the commit skips the ladder and deploy-review checks. This is the "weakening through config" invariant. (3) Cheapest fix: move the `HARD_PATHS` check above the `exclude` check so hard paths always win. Full fix: reject or ignore any `exclude` entry that matches or covers a HARD_PATH, record an audit entry for the attempt, and add a regression test. (gate.py:20)
medium

Type and shape of `exclude` are not validated, so a malformed config fails open. (1) The attacker must already control config content. For example, `exclude: "gate.py deploy.py"` as a string, or `exclude: null`, or a non-dict config. (2) With a string, `path in str` becomes a substring match, so a single string can exclude arbitrary paths. With `null` or a non-dict config, a TypeError or AttributeError is raised, and its handling is unknown, which may be fail-open. Paths are also compared without normalization (`./x`, `a//b`, case on darwin), which lets them slip past or past HARD_PATHS. (3) Cheapest fix: `excl = config.get('exclude') if isinstance(config, dict) else None`, and if the result is not a `list[str]`, fall back to strict mode with an empty exclude set. Full fix: schema validation for the config, plus normalizing paths (posix-normpath relative to the repo root) before any comparison. (gate.py:20)
medium

Excluding a path via config is a silent skip with no audit-log entry. (1) The attacker must already be able to edit config. (2) They gain an invisible narrowing of gate coverage: nothing in the audit shows that a path was removed from checking. (3) Cheapest fix: write an audit record (the path and the source `exclude`) when the `return False` branch is taken. Full fix: surface the active exclusions in the deploy diff and summary. (gate.py:21)
medium

The new branch ships without a test. The diff contains no test covering (a) exclude on a regular path, (b) an attempt to exclude a HARD_PATH, which must stay True, and (c) a broken, missing, or non-list `exclude`. (1) No attacker is needed; this is a regression risk. (2) A future reordering would reintroduce the fail-open unnoticed. (3) Cheapest fix: one parametrized test on `is_code_path` covering all three cases. Full fix: also add a mutation check proving the test turns red when the check order is swapped. (gate.py:20)
critical

Config-controlled `command` now reaches `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`, a shell-injection sink explicitly blocking under AGENTS.md's gate security class (repeat of the 25.07 `_run_empirical` finding). (1) Precondition: the attacker only needs write access to the config the runner reads, such as a repo-local `.codex-gate.yaml` or an unstaged or worktree edit, which a malicious PR or reviewed-side branch already has. (2) Gain: arbitrary shell execution with the gate user's privileges via `;`, `&&`, `$(...)`, backticks or redirection. That allows bypassing or forging gate verdicts, ledger or audit writes, and code execution on the deploy host, so a fail-open gate across all plugin users. (3) Cheapest fix: revert to `subprocess.run(shlex.split(config['command']), shell=False)`. Full fix: require `command` to be an argv list validated against an allowlist of certified binaries resolved from the plugin directory (not PATH or worktree), and reject strings entirely. (runner.py:5)
medium

No regression test for this change. There is no test proving that shell metacharacters in `config['command']` are passed as literal argv and not interpreted, which is how this regression got through. (1) Precondition: none beyond a future edit to runner.py. (2) Gain: shell-injection regressions return silently. (3) Cheapest fix: add a test with a harmless payload such as `command: "true; touch <tmp>/pwned"`, asserting the marker file is not created and `shell` is False. Per R-GUARD-TEST-MUST-BE-HARMLESS-UNARMED, the payload must write only to tmp_path. Full fix: mutation-test that the assertion fails when `shell=True` is restored. (runner.py:5)
critical

Removing 'gpt-5.6-sol' leaves claude-opus-5 as the sole BLOCKING_PANEL reviewer, turning the gate into Anthropic self-review. This violates the AGENTS.md invariant that Claude cannot be the only blocking reviewer. (1) The attacker needs only commit access to reviewers.py, or a Claude-authored change landing it. (2) They gain approval of Claude-authored code, including later gate-weakening diffs, by a same-family reviewer with no cross-family union. (3) Cheapest fix: revert and restore 'gpt-5.6-sol'. Full fix: have the panel loader fail closed unless at least two model families, including one non-Anthropic, are present. (reviewers.py:9)
medium

No test pins the cross-family composition of BLOCKING_PANEL, so this weakening would pass the suite silently. (1) The attacker needs the same repo write access as above. (2) They gain removal of the second family without any red test. (3) Cheapest fix: add an assertion that the panel contains a non-Anthropic family. Full fix: a mutation-tested invariant test plus a runtime check at gate startup. (reviewers.py:9)
high

A hardcoded credential-shaped token is written into the audit log on every review call, which the constitution's security class names as blocking ("secret or token in audit"). (1) The attacker must already have read access to the audit log, or to anywhere it is shipped (inframon, backups, CI artifacts). (2) They gain a key-shaped secret that is also committed to source, so it leaks through the repo itself. Every audit line also normalizes secrets in audit, and scanners and redaction rules tuned to that prefix will fire or be trained around it. (3) Cheapest fix: delete the literal from the audit string. Full fix: route `audit()` through a redaction layer that masks key-like patterns, rotate the value if it was ever real, and add a test asserting audit output never contains the key. (gate.py:31)
medium

The raw `response` is interpolated verbatim into the audit record. (1) The attacker must already have audit-log read access, or be able to shape the reviewer response. (2) They gain any tokens, echoed request data or verdict payloads the response carries. A reviewer-controlled response can also inject newlines or forged fields into an append-only audit log, which weakens audit integrity. (3) Cheapest fix: log only a status or verdict field plus a hash of the response. Full fix: structured, escaped audit records with an allowlist of fields. (gate.py:31)
medium

The audit line records a fixed literal instead of anything derived from the real `api_key` argument. (1) The attacker must already have a position where they rely on audit to reconstruct which credential was used. (2) They gain misattribution: the audit trail claims a key that was never used, so key-compromise forensics are misled. (3) Cheapest fix: log a non-reversible fingerprint of `api_key`, such as the last 4 characters or a short hash. Full fix: a centralized credential-fingerprint helper used by all gates. (gate.py:31)
low

The new audit path in `request_review` has no test covering it, so neither the redaction behavior nor the record format is pinned. (1) The attacker must already be positioned to make a future edit. (2) They gain a silent regression that reintroduces secret logging. (3) Cheapest fix: add one test asserting the audit output contains neither the key nor the key prefix. Full fix: a conftest-wide audit capture fixture with a secret-pattern assertion. (gate.py:31)
critical

Fail-open: a provider outage (TimeoutError/OSError) is now reported as status 'ok' with verdict 'approve', so an unreviewed change passes the blocking gate as if it were clean. (1) Attacker must already control: only the ability to make the reviewer call fail, such as a network block, DNS or proxy tampering, a firewall rule, an exhausted quota that surfaces as OSError, or simply waiting for a natural outage; no gate or config access is needed. (2) Gains: a deploy or commit is certified as reviewed without any review. This silently defeats the mandatory two-family panel, because the missing member's slot is filled with a synthetic approve, and it leaves no audit trail distinguishing it from a real review. (3) Cheapest fix: revert to `ReviewRun(status='unavailable')`, and make sure callers treat anything other than 'ok' as a block. Full fix: add a regression test asserting that an injected TimeoutError/OSError yields a non-ok status and a blocking outcome, and record provider-unavailable events in the audit log. (reviewer.py:43)
medium

No test covers the changed except-branch. The outage path is exactly where fail-closed semantics must be pinned by a test; without one, this regression (or a future one) can land unnoticed. (1) Attacker must already control: nothing, since this is a process gap. (2) Gains: a future silent reintroduction of fail-open. (3) Cheapest fix: a single unit test that monkeypatches `call_provider` to raise TimeoutError and OSError and asserts the result is not approve. Full fix: parametrize the test over all exception classes the provider can raise, including unexpected ones, and assert the gate blocks on each. (reviewer.py:42)
